out: Choose the right firewall type and write basic rules.
Distinguish IDS from IPS, and network from host-based sensors.
Explain content filtering and network access control.
plain: A firewall is a guard checking addresses and door numbers. A web application firewall reads the content of what is being carried. An intrusion detection system is a security camera with an alarm, and an intrusion prevention system is a guard who can actually step in.
tech: Segmentation limits movement between areas of a network. Access controls decide who may reach what. Firewalls include rule-based filtering, which permits or denies according to a list; Layer 4 firewalls, which decide on addresses, ports and connection state; and Layer 7 firewalls, which understand applications. A web application firewall (WAF) protects web applications from attacks such as injection. Unified threat management (UTM) combines several functions in one device. Rate-limiting requests restricts how many requests are allowed in a period, which slows brute force and some denial-of-service attempts.

An intrusion detection system (IDS) monitors and alerts. An intrusion prevention system (IPS) sits inline and can block. Network-based intrusion detection system (NIDS) and network-based intrusion prevention system (NIPS) sensors watch network traffic. Host-based intrusion detection system (HIDS) and host-based intrusion prevention system (HIPS) agents watch a single host. A wireless intrusion prevention system (WIPS) detects and responds to wireless threats such as rogue access points. Detection may use signatures, which match known patterns, or anomalies, which flag departures from normal.

A content filter controls what users can reach or send. Data loss prevention (DLP) detects and blocks sensitive data leaving. Agent-based filters run on the device and work anywhere. A centralized proxy routes traffic through a central inspection point.

Network access control (NAC) decides whether a device may join a network. It uses 802.1X for port-based authentication, usually with a RADIUS server, endpoint posture and compliance checks such as patch level, and captive portals, the web pages that appear before guest Wi-Fi access. Monitoring and alerting tell you when these controls see something important.
terms: Dividing a network to limit movement.
Mechanisms that decide who may reach what.
Watching systems and notifying people about important events.
A firewall that permits or denies according to an ordered list.
A firewall that decides using addresses, ports and connection state.
A firewall that understands application content.
Web application firewall: protects web applications.
Unified threat management: several security functions in one device.
Restricting the number of requests in a period.
A control that limits access to or movement of content.
Data loss prevention: stops sensitive data from leaving.
Using software installed on the device.
A central point through which traffic is inspected.
Network access control: decides which devices may connect.
A standard for port-based network authentication.
Whether a device meets security requirements.
Web pages shown before network access is granted.
A protocol for centralized authentication, often used with 802.1X.
eg: A login page is rate-limited to five attempts a minute for each IP address, which slows guessing.
A laptop missing critical patches is placed by NAC into a remediation network until it is updated.

walks.title: Read a firewall rule list
steps: Rules are evaluated from top to bottom, and the first match wins.
Rule 1: allow TCP 443 from any source to the web server.
Rule 2: allow TCP 22 from the admin subnet to the web server.
Rule 3: deny everything else, and log it.
A broad allow rule placed above a specific deny rule will defeat it, so order matters.

labs.title: Write and test firewall rules
labs.tool: ufw in your lab VM; the firewall PBQ in Atlas
do: In your VM, run sudo ufw reset, then set default deny incoming and default allow outgoing.
Allow TCP 443 from anywhere, and TCP 22 only from a subnet of your choice. Then run sudo ufw enable.
Run sudo ufw status numbered. Explain each rule aloud.
Complete the firewall exercise under Performance-based practice in Atlas.
Finally, run sudo ufw disable or restore your snapshot.
labs.expect: Your rule list shows exactly the intended permissions.
labs.explain: Stating the purpose of each rule is good practice, because rules with no known reason build up over time and become risk.
pass: Your VM's rule list is correct.
You scored 80% or more on the firewall exercise.

qs.s: What is the key difference between an IDS and an IPS?

a.t: An IPS can block traffic, and an IDS only alerts
a.w: The IPS sits inline and can act.

a.t: An IPS can only be used on Wi-Fi

qs.s: Which control best stops cross-site scripting aimed at a web application?

a.w: It sees only ports, addresses and connection state.

qs.s: A device is checked for patches and antivirus before it may join the network. What is this?

a.t: Network access control using endpoint posture
a.w: NAC can check compliance before granting access.

qs.s: An ordered list reads: 1) allow any to any on TCP 443; 2) deny 203.0.113.9 to any on TCP 443. What happens to 203.0.113.9?

a.t: It is allowed, because rule 1 matches first
a.w: First match wins, so rule 2 is never reached.

a.t: It is denied, because deny rules always take priority
a.w: Most firewalls process rules in order.

a.t: It is logged and dropped automatically
a.w: Nothing in this list would do that.

a.t: The firewall will report a syntax error

mistakes: Thinking a firewall can stop every web attack.
Placing a broad allow rule above a narrow deny rule.
sum: Firewalls enforce rules, and WAFs inspect web content.
IDS detects, and IPS can block.
NAC decides what devices may join.

lessons.title: Network controls: firewalls, IDS and IPS, content filters and NAC
lessons.why: These are the everyday tools of a security team. Knowing which one fits a scenario is a major part of this domain, and PBQs often ask you to configure them.
lessons.scenario: A web application is receiving SQL injection attempts. The network firewall already allows only port 443. Which control is most appropriate to add?
lessons.answer: A web application firewall, which inspects the contents of web requests. A Layer 4 firewall permits port 443 and cannot see the attack within. Secure coding should also be applied.

product: Network controls appear in products as IP allow lists, rate-limit errors and web application firewall block pages. An over-eager firewall rule can stop a genuine customer, who then sees an unexplained error. A reference code on the block page lets support help them.

eng: What does a user see when the WAF or a rate limit blocks them?
sec: How would a false positive be reported and resolved?
prod: Which customers need IP allow lists, and who manages them?

design.noex: Firewalls are mostly technical knowledge, so the useful step is designing clear block states with your engineers.

out: Explain sandboxing, application control and MDM.
plain: Antivirus is a list of known criminals' photos. Endpoint detection and response is a detective watching for suspicious behaviour and able to intervene. Allow listing is a guest list: if your name is not on it, you do not get in. A sandbox is a quarantine room for testing a suspicious package.
tech: Hardening removes unnecessary services, accounts and settings. Sandboxing runs code in an isolated environment. Application control restricts what software runs, through allow lists, which permit only approved items, or block lists, which forbid known bad items. Allow lists are stronger but need more upkeep.

Antivirus detects known malicious code and some suspicious behaviour. Endpoint detection and response (EDR) records endpoint activity, detects suspicious behaviour and enables a response such as isolating a host. Extended detection and response (XDR) correlates data across endpoints, networks, identity and email.

Mobile device management (MDM) enforces policies such as passcodes and encryption, can remotely wipe a lost device and controls apps. In Windows domains, Group Policy centrally applies settings to users and computers. Security-Enhanced Linux (SELinux) is a mandatory access control system that confines what each process can do, even if it runs as a privileged account.
terms: Reducing attack surface through secure settings.
Running code in an isolated environment.
Lists of items that are explicitly permitted.
Lists of items that are explicitly forbidden.
Software that detects known malicious code and behaviours.
Endpoint detection and response: detects and responds on endpoints.
Extended detection and response: correlates data across many sources.
Mobile device management: central control of mobile devices.
Windows feature that centrally applies settings.
Security-Enhanced Linux: mandatory access control for Linux.
eg: EDR notices Word launching PowerShell and isolates that laptop from the network, automatically.
A lost phone is remotely wiped using MDM.

walks.title: Choose between allow list and block list
steps: If the environment is stable, like a kiosk or a server, consider an allow list.
If users constantly need new software, a block list is easier but is weaker.
Plan how updates are handled, since a new version can break a hash-based allow list.
Apply the change using change management, and monitor what gets blocked.

labs.title: Check SELinux or AppArmor and build a sandbox habit
do: In Ubuntu, run sudo aa-status to see AppArmor, Ubuntu's mandatory access control.
If you have a Fedora or RHEL VM, run sestatus to view SELinux, and ls -Z to see file labels.
Identify one confined program, and what it is confining.
Write down how you would use a snapshot-based VM as a sandbox for an unknown file.
labs.expect: A list of confined profiles, and a safe written procedure.
labs.explain: Mandatory access control limits even privileged processes, which is why compromises of confined services can stay contained.
pass: You viewed profile or SELinux status.
Your sandbox procedure includes isolation and snapshot restore.

qs.s: Which approach permits only approved software?

a.w: This handles network access for guests.

qs.s: What does EDR add beyond traditional antivirus?

a.t: Continuous behaviour monitoring and response actions such as host isolation
a.w: EDR is designed for detection and response.
EDR is not limited to signatures.

a.w: MDM can erase the device remotely.
This is for Linux access control.

a.t: SELinux confines the process by policy

Assuming a block list stops new malware.
sum: EDR adds behaviour-based detection and response.
Allow lists are stronger, and block lists are easier.
MDM, Group Policy and SELinux centralize or enforce control.

Correlation across endpoints, network, identity and email.

lessons.title: Securing endpoints, mobile devices and operating systems
lessons.why: Most attacks end up on an endpoint. Stronger endpoint visibility and tighter control over what can run are often the difference between a blocked attack and a breach.
lessons.scenario: A company's kiosks should run one application and nothing else. Which control provides the strongest enforcement?
lessons.answer: Application allow listing, as nothing outside the approved list can run. Block lists would miss anything unknown.

product: Device management reaches product design through conditional access: "this device is not compliant" is a confusing message for a user who cannot fix it. Mobile policies can also block copy and paste or screenshots inside a managed app.

eng: Which device signals does our product actually receive?
sec: Which device states should block access entirely?
prod: Who helps an employee whose device becomes non-compliant?

design.noex: Endpoint controls are mostly operated by IT. The useful design contribution is clear messaging, which the next exercises practice.

out: Explain how SPF, DKIM, DMARC and BIMI work together.
plain: Input validation is like checking that a phone number field has only digits before accepting it. SPF is a list of who may send mail for your domain, DKIM is a wax seal on the letter, and DMARC tells recipients what to do if either one fails. A honeypot is a decoy safe left out to catch thieves.
tech: Application security covers input validation, which checks data against what is expected; secure cookies, using the Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite attributes; static code analysis, which reviews source code without running it; and code signing, which proves who published code and that it has not been altered. Repositories should use secrets scanning to find leaked credentials.

Email security uses DNS records. Sender Policy Framework (SPF) lists the servers allowed to send for a domain. DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) adds a digital signature to messages. Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) tells recipients how to handle messages failing checks, such as none, quarantine or reject, and asks for reports. Brand Indicators for Message Identification (BIMI) displays a verified brand logo, and depends on DMARC enforcement.

Deception and disruption technology includes a honeypot (a decoy system), a honeynet (a network of decoys), a honeyfile (a decoy document), a honeytoken (fake data or a credential that raises an alert when used) and a canary account (a decoy account that should never be used). Any use of these indicates something is wrong, so false positives are low.

Cookies protected using attributes such as Secure and HttpOnly.
Reviewing code for flaws without running it.
Digitally signing code to prove its origin and integrity.
Stores of source code and related files.
Searching code and repositories for exposed credentials.

DomainKeys Identified Mail: signs outgoing mail.

Fake data that raises an alert when used.
A decoy account that should never be used.

eg: A domain publishes a DMARC policy of reject, so forged mail claiming to be from the domain is refused by receiving servers.
A fake credentials file on a file share triggers an alert the moment anyone opens it.

walks.title: Read a domain's email security
steps: Look up the SPF TXT record, starting v=spf1.
Look up the DMARC record at _dmarc.domain.
Check the DMARC policy: p=none only monitors, while p=reject is enforcing.
Check whether messages carry a DKIM-Signature header.

labs.title: Inspect email authentication
labs.tool: nslookup, and your own mail client
do: Run nslookup -type=txt followed by a large public domain, and find an SPF record.
Run nslookup -type=txt _dmarc.domain for the same domain, and note its policy.
In your own mailbox, open a message's full headers and find the Authentication-Results line.
Note whether SPF, DKIM and DMARC passed.
labs.expect: An SPF record, a DMARC policy and pass or fail results in a real message.
labs.explain: These results are what mail systems use to decide on spoofed messages.
pass: You identified an SPF record and a DMARC policy.
You read SPF and DKIM results in a header.

What does a DMARC policy of p=reject do?

a.w: This is the strongest policy setting.

lessons.title: Application, email and deception controls
lessons.why: Web applications and email are the two most common ways into an organization. Deception gives defenders a rare advantage, since nobody legitimate should touch a decoy.
lessons.scenario: Attackers keep spoofing a company's domain in phishing emails to its customers. Which control lets the company instruct receiving servers to reject those messages?
lessons.answer: DMARC with a policy of reject, supported by correctly configured SPF and DKIM.

product: Sending email from a customer's own domain requires SPF, DKIM and DMARC records, which is a difficult task to hand to a marketing manager. Products that handle this well turn a technical protocol into a guided, verifiable setup, and they say plainly what is at risk if it stays incomplete.

eng: How do we check the records, and how often?
What happens to mail while the setup is incomplete?
sec: What is the recommended DMARC policy progression for customers?
prod: Who at a customer usually has access to DNS?

ex.title: Design an email authentication setup wizard
ex.scenario: An email marketing product lets customers send from their own domain. Many customers skip authentication, and their mail ends up in spam or can be spoofed.
ex.problem: The current settings page lists DNS records with no explanation, and the person using it is often not the person who controls DNS.
tasks: Explain SPF, DKIM and DMARC in plain language within the flow.
Design the setup with a hand-off to a DNS administrator.
Design verification, propagation wait, partial success and failure states.
Show the path from a monitoring DMARC policy to enforcement.
constraints: DNS changes can take time to propagate and the product cannot speed them up.
Moving to a reject policy too early can block legitimate mail.
Records must be copied exactly, so manual retyping should be avoided.
needs: Marketers need to know what to ask for, and from whom.
DNS administrators need exact values with no marketing context.
Account owners need to see the risk of leaving setup unfinished.
ex.deliver: A setup wizard flow, a hand-off page and a state list covering verification.

crit.t: The flow represents SPF, DKIM and DMARC correctly and in the right order.
The design explains the harm of spoofing and of an early reject policy.
A non-technical user can complete their part and hand off the rest.
The design defines success in terms of authenticated mail, and not of completed screens.

seniors: A setup step that depends on another team needs a designed hand-off, because the product loses the user at that point.
Confirm the recommended policy timing with deliverability experts.

cq.s: Which step should a setup wizard recommend first for a domain with an unknown sending landscape?

a.t: Start DMARC in monitoring mode and review reports
a.w: This reveals legitimate senders before anything is blocked.

a.t: Publish DMARC with an immediate reject policy today
a.w: Legitimate mail from unknown senders could be blocked.

a.t: Remove all SPF records before adding any DKIM keys
a.w: This removes existing protection and breaks authentication.

a.t: Wait until spoofing has been reported by customers
a.w: Waiting leaves the domain exposed and gives no data.

out: Follow an asset through its life cycle.
Explain why an accurate inventory matters.
plain: Think of a company car. It is planned, bought, assigned to a driver, tracked and serviced, then sold or scrapped. You would clear out the glove compartment before selling it. Hardware, software and data need the same care.
tech: The asset management life cycle has these stages. Planning/scoping decides what is needed. The acquisition/procurement process covers buying through approved suppliers, with security requirements. Assignment/accounting records who owns or uses an asset and adds it to inventory. Monitoring/asset tracking keeps records current, for example through discovery scans. Disposal/decommissioning retires an asset securely.

NIST SP 800-88 describes three main sanitization outcomes: clear, using logical methods to protect against simple recovery; purge, using stronger techniques that defeat laboratory recovery, such as cryptographic erase; and destroy, making the media unusable. Keep a certificate of destruction when third parties do this work. Data assets need the same tracking and also have owners, classifications and retention periods. Software assets need license and version tracking.
terms: The stages an asset goes through, from planning to disposal.
Deciding what is needed and what is included.
Recording ownership and adding to inventory.
Keeping track of where assets are and their state.
Destroying the key so that encrypted data cannot be recovered.
eg: A forgotten test server, not on any inventory, runs out-of-date software and becomes the entry point for a breach.
An organization resells old laptops without wiping them, and customer data ends up on the second-hand market.

walks.title: Decommission a server
steps: Confirm its owner approves retirement, and check dependencies.
Migrate or archive data according to retention rules.
Revoke its credentials and certificates and remove its DNS and firewall entries.
Sanitize or destroy the disks in accordance with data sensitivity.
Update the inventory and keep the record.

labs.title: Build a small asset register
do: Record ten assets you own: devices, software and data sets.
For each, add owner, location, classification and end-of-support date.
Mark the disposal method you would use.
Find the end-of-support date for your OS on the vendor's site.
labs.expect: A register that shows which assets are near or past end of support.
labs.explain: An up-to-date register is the base of patching, incident response and audits.
pass: Your register has all fields for ten assets.

qs.s: Why is an accurate asset inventory important?

a.t: You cannot protect or patch what you do not know exists
It replaces the need for firewalls
It removes the need for backups

qs.s: Put the stages of the asset life cycle in order.
qs.why: Each stage relies on records from the one before.

qs.s: Which sanitization result protects against laboratory recovery while still allowing reuse?

a.w: Purge defeats laboratory techniques, and the media can be reused.
Clear protects only against simple recovery.
The media cannot be reused after this.

qs.s: A server is retired, but its service account stays active. What risk results?

a.t: A stale credential remains that could be abused

mistakes: Assuming that deleting files or formatting a drive destroys the data.
Tracking hardware but forgetting data and software.
sum: Assets need an owner at every stage.
Dispose of media according to data sensitivity.
cards: Name the NIST media sanitization outcomes.
Destroying the encryption key so that encrypted data cannot be recovered.
lessons.title: Managing hardware, software and data assets
lessons.why: You cannot protect what you do not know you have. Assets that nobody tracks do not get patched, and discarded drives have exposed a surprising amount of sensitive data.
lessons.scenario: A company is retiring encrypted SSDs that held confidential data, and wants to reuse them within the company. What is an appropriate method?
lessons.answer: Purge using cryptographic erase, then verify. Destroying them would prevent reuse, and clearing alone may not be enough for confidential data on SSDs.

product: Asset inventories appear as device lists, app inventories and connected-app pages. A product can only help someone secure what it can show them, so an accurate, searchable inventory with ownership and last-seen dates is itself a security feature.

eng: How current is this inventory, and what is missing from it?
sec: Which assets are most critical, and do we show that?
prod: Who owns an asset when its owner leaves?

design.noex: Asset management informs dashboards you will design in Week 11.
